replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what an AI chatbot is, in plain words. Keep it short, then let me try one.
replies.raw:
Welcome. I'm Merc, a chatbot in a learning app built to help people get comfortable with AI.

You can't break anything here, and there are no silly questions. If something goes wrong, we start again.

Type in the box at the bottom, or tap the microphone on your keyboard and talk. Then tap the arrow to send.

An AI chatbot is a computer program you talk to by typing or speaking. It writes back in plain words.

No one is typing back to you — it's all the program.

[KEY]An AI chatbot is a computer program that writes back to you, not a person.[/KEY]

Try asking me: "Are you a real person?"

replies.user: Are you a real person?
replies.raw:
No. I'm Merc, a chatbot in a learning app. No one is typing back to you.

Practicing on me works the same way as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot.

Notice that I answered right away, any time of day — that's one thing chatbots are good for.

Now ask me anything you're curious about. It can be about cooking, your garden, or a place you'd like to visit.

replies.user: How do I keep basil alive on a windowsill?
replies.raw:
Basil loves sun, so a south-facing window is ideal. It needs at least 6 hours of light a day.

Water it when the top inch of soil feels dry. Don't let it sit in water — empty the saucer after watering.

Pinch off any flowers as soon as you see them, because once it flowers, the leaves turn bitter.

Notice how asking about your own basil got you a specific, useful answer — that's how chatbots work best.

Chatbots like this one learned from a huge amount of writing. Each answer is built by guessing, word by word, what fits best.

It isn't a person, and it isn't a search engine. There are many: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot.

Merc is one too, and what you learn here works in all of them.

[KEY]A chatbot guesses the best words to write back — it isn't looking up a right answer.[/KEY]

Tap the answer you think is right. There's no grade.

[Q]
Which is the best description of an AI chatbot?
A) A person at the company typing answers to you
B) A computer program that writes answers by guessing what words fit best
C) A big library of facts that looks up the right answer every time
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A computer program that writes answers by guessing what words fit best
replies.raw:
That's exactly right.

You asked about your own basil, and that's how to get good help from a chatbot.

One thing to keep in mind: if you wouldn't write something on a postcard for anyone to read, don't type it into a chatbot.

Try this today: Ask a chatbot one thing you've wondered about this week.

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 3] Teach me what I should never share with an AI chatbot, and why. Then let me practice asking for help safely.
replies.raw:
Last time, you asked a chatbot to say something in plain words.

Some things are safer to keep off the screen entirely. Think of it like a postcard: anyone could read it on the way.

[KEY]If you wouldn't write it on a postcard, don't type it into a chatbot.[/KEY]

Here's what to leave out:

- Passwords and PINs
- One-time codes (the code a company texts you)
- Bank or card numbers
- Social Security, Medicare or other ID numbers
- Medical records
- Photos of your ID, Medicare or insurance card
- Other people's private details

A general detail, like "I'm allergic to nuts", is fine. You can almost always get good help without the private part.

Try asking me: "My bank charged me twice. What should I do?"

replies.user: My bank charged me twice. What should I do?
replies.raw:
Here are some steps to take:

1. Check your statement to confirm the duplicate charge.
2. Call your bank using the number on the back of your card or on your statement.
3. Tell them the date and amount of the charge, and ask them to reverse the duplicate.
4. Ask for a confirmation number or email when they fix it.

Notice that you didn't need your account number to get good help.

Your chats are usually saved, and some companies use them to improve their AI. To control this, look for the settings or privacy option in any chatbot app, or use a temporary chat if it offers one.

[KEY]The safest step is to leave private details out in the first place.[/KEY]

[EX]Google tells people who use Gemini not to type anything confidential they wouldn't want a reviewer to see. ChatGPT and Claude let people choose whether their chats help improve the AI.[/EX]

Which one is safe to type into a chatbot?

[Q]
Which one is safe to type into a chatbot?
A) "Is Rosebud1952 a strong password?"
B) "How do I make a strong password I can remember?"
C) The code your bank texted you a minute ago, so it can explain it
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) "How do I make a strong password I can remember?"
replies.raw:
That's right. Option B gets you useful help without giving anything away.

You asked for general advice, and that's exactly how to stay safe while still getting what you need.

The postcard rule works in every chatbot: if you wouldn't write it on a postcard, don't type it into a chatbot.

Next time you ask a chatbot for help, leave out names and numbers, and see if the help is still good.

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 4] Teach me about AI voice-clone and family emergency scams, and exactly what to do if I get one of those calls. Then help me make a plan.
replies.raw:
Last time, you learned the postcard rule.

AI can copy someone's voice from a short recording — even a video posted online. Scammers use that to call you sounding exactly like a grandchild or other relative.

Even if their name or number shows on your screen, callers can fake that too.

The warning signs come fast:

- It's urgent.
- It's a secret ("don't tell Mom").
- They want cash, gift cards, or money sent from your bank.
- Sometimes someone comes to your door to pick up cash.

[EX]In 2023, an Arizona mother got a call. Her 15-year-old daughter was safe the whole time. But a voice that sounded exactly like her daughter asked for help, and a man demanded money. The mother later told the U.S. Senate about it.[/EX]

A **code word** is a word only your family knows. If a caller can't say it, hang up.

Try asking me: "Write a text asking my family to pick a code word."

replies.user: Write a text asking my family to pick a code word.
replies.raw:
Here's a text you can send:

---

"Hey everyone — I just learned about a scam where AI can fake someone's voice to sound like a family member calling for help. I'd like us to pick a secret code word.

If any of us ever calls in an emergency, we say the word so everyone knows it's really us. Can we agree on one this week?"

---

Notice that the text explains why, so your family is more likely to take it seriously.

Don't tell me the actual code word. Keep that for your family.

Now try: "Make it short and friendly."

replies.user: Make it short and friendly.
replies.raw:
Here's a shorter version:

---

"Hey family! I learned a tip about staying safe from phone scams. Can we pick a secret code word — just for us? If someone calls in an emergency, they say the word so we know it's really them.

Let's pick one this week!"

---

Same idea, but lighter and easier to read.

Now, the most important part: what to do when a call comes in.

**Hang up and call back.** Call the person from your contacts, or on a number you already know.

If you can't reach them, call someone else in the family — even if the caller said to keep it secret.

Hanging up won't hurt them. If it's real, they'll still be okay in the five minutes it takes to check.

[Q]
A call sounds exactly like your grandson. He's crying, says he's in jail, and asks you to buy gift cards and keep it secret. What do you do first?
A) Buy the gift cards so he's safe
B) Hang up and call him, or his parents, on a number you already know
C) Ask the caller for a phone number to call him back
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Hang up and call him, or his parents, on a number you already know
replies.raw:
That's exactly right.

You spotted the trap too: a number the caller gives you goes straight back to the scammer.

You now have a real plan — a code word your family picks, and a clear first step when a call feels wrong.

Don't trust the voice. Hang up, then call back on a number you already know.

Try this today: Send the code-word text to your family.

Last time, you had a chatbot write an email and copied it out.

Confusing letters often have hard words and hidden deadlines. A chatbot can explain both in plain language.

The key is to share only the confusing part. Cover your name, address, account number, and any ID numbers with a piece of paper before you take a photo.

Or type only the tricky paragraph, leaving your details out.

[KEY]Cover your name and numbers before sharing any letter with a chatbot.[/KEY]

Then ask: "What does this mean, and what do I need to do?"

- An electric company's rate change

**Sunrise Health Plan: Notice of Change.** Starting January 1, your yearly deductible for Tier 3 and Tier 4 drugs will change from $250 to $400.

After you meet the deductible, you will pay 25% of the cost of specialty-tier drugs. If you want to change plans, you must do so during the Annual Enrollment Period, October 15 to December 7.

replies.user: What does this mean, and what do I need to do?
replies.raw:
Here's what this letter is saying:

Your plan is raising the amount you pay for certain drugs before your coverage kicks in. A deductible is the amount you pay each year before the plan starts paying its share.

Yours goes from $250 to $400 for Tier 3 and Tier 4 drugs, which are mid-range and higher-cost drugs.

After that, you'll pay 25% of the cost of specialty-tier drugs. Those are the most expensive kind.

If you're happy with this plan, you don't need to do anything.

If you want to compare other plans, you have a window to do that.

Notice how asking one clear question got you a plain-language breakdown of every hard term.

For this made-up letter, the deadline to switch plans is December 7.

That's the end of the Annual Enrollment Period, which runs October 15 to December 7.

Some people can switch at other times too. Your state's free Medicare helpers, called SHIP, can tell you what applies to you.

Now, one important step before you use this with your real letter: before acting on anything about money or benefits, call the sender yourself. Use the number on your Medicare card, a past bill, or the plan's official website.

Never use a number from a surprise letter or email.
